name: The Silver Maple of the Oosterpoortsgracht
age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from a registered planting date of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (Bomenstichting), entry nr 1690973
transport: In the Oosterplantsoen, a short walk from Hoorn town centre, alongside the city's other protected park trees.
story:
A fungal infection is climbing this maple from the roots up. Inspectors recorded a substantial infection at the base and root collar in 2024, on a silver maple the municipality planted between 1900 and 1910 at the water's edge of the Oosterpoortsgracht, inside the Oosterplantsoen. It is still alive and still carries a full crown, and it sits on Hoorn's own signed tree route through the park, a few dozen metres from several of the city's other protected trees.

The park itself is younger than its trees look. When Hoorn's city walls, gates and towers came down through the nineteenth century, the cleared ground became a walking park, and part of the old rampart still runs beneath the grass. This maple went into that new ground within its first decade.

Nobody has measured its girth, and the municipal survey gives only the planting decade rather than a year. What it does say plainly is the one thing worth knowing before a visit: the tree is in decline. See it while it is still the tree the register calls fine.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing opposite a numbered lamp post at the water's edge of the Oosterpoortsgracht. It stands inside the Oosterplantsoen, a few dozen metres from the park's other protected trees.

name: The Gray Poplar of Wilhelminapark
age_estimate: roughly 75 to 90 years, sources disagree between a 1935 and a 1950 planting

location.address: West side of the pond, Wilhelminapark, Emmalaan, Hoorn

verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (Bomenstichting), entry nr 1690981
transport: In Wilhelminapark on Emmalaan, a short walk from Hoorn town centre.
story:
Storms have torn real damage into this poplar's crown, and it has kept growing anyway: inspectors call its overall condition good despite it. The trunk is just over four metres round, a serious size for a species that rarely gets the chance to grow old in a Dutch park.

Wilhelminapark itself dates to 1950, laid out by the garden architect J.H.R. van Koolwijk and named for Queen Wilhelmina the same year, next to the Oranjebuurt neighbourhood then under construction. The tree's own planting date is disputed even by the sources that recorded it: the municipal survey suggests it went in with the park in 1950, then adds that other records put it nearer 1935, fifteen years earlier. Either reading makes it one of the older plantings on this stretch of the pond's west bank.

Gray poplars hybridise readily with white poplar and aspen, and a trunk this size on a tree still holding a full, storm-battered crown is exactly the kind the species is protected for here. It stands free to see on the western side of the park's pond, on Emmalaan.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, just over four metres round, and by real storm damage still visible in the crown. It stands on the west side of the pond in Wilhelminapark, on Emmalaan.

name: The Lime of the Noorderplantsoen

location.address: Noorderplantsoen, opposite the railway station, Noorderstraat, Hoorn

verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (Bomenstichting), entry nr 1683821
transport: In the Noorderplantsoen directly opposite Hoorn's railway station.
story:
This lime went into the ground the year Wilhelmina was crowned. The Noorderplantsoen itself is barely older: it was laid out over a stretch of filled-in city moat between the Spoorstraat and the Kleine Noord as Hoorn built its railway station, which opened in 1882, and the lime was planted in 1898 to mark the young queen's coronation.

After 1915 the park's oldest trees were cleared and replanted, and this lime is one of the survivors from that first planting rather than one of the replacements. It stands behind its own small fence, a jubilee railing put up around the trunk and root base for extra protection, with open ground clear around it.

Nobody has recorded which lime species it is more precisely than the Dutch word for lime in general, and this page will not guess narrower than the source does. If you know, tell us.

It stands in the plantsoen directly opposite Hoorn's railway station, a few minutes from the Noorderstraat.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small jubilee fence ringing its trunk and root base, standing in open ground. It stands in the Noorderplantsoen directly opposite Hoorn's railway station.

name: The Last Elms of Park Baadland
age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from a registered planting date of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (Bomenstichting), entry nr 1682399
transport: On the small artificial peninsula of Park Baadland, about a 15 minute walk south of Hoorn town centre.
story:
Twenty Dutch elms went into Park Baadland between 1900 and 1910, and two are left standing. Dutch elm disease took the other eighteen in stages: nine still stood in a 2008 survey, and by 2026 the count was down to these two.

Baadland is an artificial peninsula, built to shield Hoorn's harbour from the open Zuiderzee before being turned into a public plantsoen between 1837 and 1842, and it has stayed parkland ever since. Herons used to nest in the crowns of its older elms; both the herons and the eighteen other trees that once held them are gone.

No source names which two of the original twenty these are or gives either one a girth, so the register's single coordinate for the park is what this page can offer rather than an exact pair of trunks. That is the honest state of a planting that has been dying for over a century and is not finished yet.

Free to see, inside the small park, a walk of about a kilometre from Hoorn's town centre.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the only two old elms left in Park Baadland, from an original planting of twenty. They stand somewhere on the small peninsula that shields Hoorn's old harbour; the pin is rough, so look for the pair.
